question: A 25-year-old man is brought to the emergency department 30 minutes after he was involved in a motorcycle collision. He was not wearing a helmet. Physical examination shows left periorbital ecchymosis. A CT scan of the head shows a fracture of the greater wing of the left sphenoid bone with compression of the left superior orbital fissure. Physical examination of this patient is most likely to show which of the following findings?

enhanced_information: The fracture of the greater wing of the left sphenoid bone with compression of the left superior orbital fissure can lead to damage of cranial nerves III, IV, VI, and V1. This results in several potential findings. The most relevant findings include: 1) Absent left corneal reflex due to involvement of the sensory component of the trigeminal nerve (V1), which is responsible for corneal sensation. 2) Numbness of the left cheek due to involvement of the maxillary nerve (V2). 3) Impaired lateral gaze on the left due to involvement of the abducens nerve (CN VI). 4) Possible ptosis and pupillary involvement due to oculomotor nerve (CN III) damage. The option of complete loss of vision of the left eye is less likely unless the optic nerve (CN II) is directly involved, which is not typically the case with this type of fracture. Therefore, the most likely physical examination finding is absent left corneal reflex.
analysis: The patient has a fracture of the greater wing of the left sphenoid bone with compression of the left superior orbital fissure, which can affect several cranial nerves. The relevant cranial nerves involved include: CN III (oculomotor), CN IV (trochlear), CN VI (abducens), and the ophthalmic branch of CN V (trigeminal). The absent left corneal reflex is due to the involvement of the sensory component of the trigeminal nerve (V1), which is responsible for corneal sensation. Numbness of the left cheek would be due to involvement of the maxillary nerve (V2), but this is not the most direct consequence of the superior orbital fissure syndrome. Preserved left lateral gaze is unlikely due to the involvement of CN VI, which controls lateral eye movement. Complete loss of vision would require direct involvement of the optic nerve (CN II), which is not typically affected in this scenario. Therefore, the most likely finding is the absent left corneal reflex due to the damage to the sensory fibers of the trigeminal nerve. This aligns with the enhanced information provided, which supports the conclusion that absent left corneal reflex is the most likely physical examination finding.
